questions.q: What does a single artificial neuron compute, mechanically?
options: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through a nonlinear activation function
A random number unrelated to its inputs
The average of all neurons in the network
A lookup in a table of stored answers
questions.explain: A neuron multiplies each input by its own weight, sums them with a bias term, and applies a nonlinear activation function to that sum — nothing more mysterious than that.

questions.q: What are the three main categories of layers in a typical neural network?
options: Training layer, testing layer, validation layer
Input layer, hidden layer(s), output layer
Weight layer, bias layer, gradient layer
Linear layer, label layer, loss layer
questions.explain: A network's structure is organized into an input layer (the feature values), one or more hidden layers, and an output layer that produces the final prediction.

questions.q: Why would stacking 100 purely linear layers (with no activation function) fail to add any extra modeling power over a single linear layer?
options: It wouldn't fail — more linear layers always add power
A weighted sum of a weighted sum is still mathematically just one weighted sum, so the whole stack collapses to a single linear function
Linear layers cannot be combined at all
Only the first layer matters; the rest are ignored
questions.explain: Without a nonlinear activation between them, composing linear layers algebraically reduces to one bigger linear layer, no matter how many you stack — the nonlinearity is what lets additional layers add real representational power.

questions.q: What is a "forward pass" in a neural network?
options: The process of adjusting every weight in the network
Pushing an input through every layer to produce a prediction — the same thing as inference
Deleting unused neurons from the network
Splitting the dataset into train and test sets
questions.explain: A forward pass computes every neuron's weighted sum and activation, layer by layer, until the output layer produces the final prediction — this is exactly what happens during inference.

questions.q: What does training a neural network actually search for?
options: The number of features in the dataset
A single global activation function shared by all networks
The values of every weight (and bias) across every connection in the network that make its predictions best match the training data
The order in which training examples are listed
questions.explain: A neural network's "knowledge" is entirely encoded in its weights; training searches for the weight values across the whole network that make the network's output best match the training data.
